_about: FRAMEWORK-BENCH-1: the named three-host comparison of roadmap item 548 (issue #1267).
One model, one task set, three hosts. The axis under test is the RUNTIME, not the model:
the claim this suite exists to check is that a mediocre model still cannot ship residue,
capability widening or unmarked emissions through the gate, which is the opposite of what
a model leaderboard measures. A high compile-rate bought by loosening G1-G9 would falsify
the claim rather than support it.
This file is the registry an outsider edits. It names the hosts, the pinned model, the task
set and the columns, so the suite can be pointed at a different endpoint or a different
The framework host is named as of the second pass. The criteria it was chosen
against are still in its entry, together with what was rejected and why, and
bench/framework_unload_survey.py re-checks every claim in those entries against

resolution_note: The roadmap and issue #1267 name the model as 'ornith-ai/Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B:Q4_K_M'.
An ollama pull from Hugging Face registers it under a longer tag carrying the registry
prefix and the -GGUF repository suffix. The two names are the same weights; the longer
one is recorded here because it is the string the endpoint answers to, and
bench/model_pin.py records which of the two a run actually resolved.
why_local: An API model drifts under a fixed name, so a reader who reruns this suite against 'the
same model' is not running the same model and the table silently re-baselines. Local
weights have a content digest, which bench/model_pin.py records, so a reader can check
that they ran what we ran instead of taking our word for it.
It also means nothing in this suite talks to a third party.
substitution_note: Any endpoint may be substituted with --endpoint/--model. The suite does not require our
model; it requires that the report say which model produced each number. A run against a
different model is a valid run of this suite and an invalid comparison against our table.

note: The 30 component specs of the syntax-2.0 acceptance benchmark. Each gives a brief plus
service interfaces to use verbatim, so the interfaces are pinned and the implementation
is the model's.
n=30 is the current task set. Issue #1205 landed tools/evolve_curriculum.py, which derives
266 tasks from repository artifacts with a computed difficulty tier; retiring n=30 in
favour of that curriculum is a named remaining gate, not something this file pretends to
have done.
Leads the table. Every other column is one revl is designed to win, so a suite whose
author picked the axes is benchmaxxing whatever the intent. What repairs it is
publishing the cost of the guarantee: the documents and constructs this project
refuses that the other hosts run without objection. If the finished table shows revl
winning every column, that is a finding about the table.

columns.note: First-pass admission rate. revl may lose this column and that is a valid result.
Leaked categories (registry / provisions / effects / listeners) after N load-unload cycles.

note: A tool or prompt attempting to exceed its declared surface. The injection
rides in the material a component reads (a service doc comment, the brief,
or the compiler output the retry loop feeds back), never in the system
prompt.
Two numbers, kept apart: compliance is how often the model does the
undeclared thing at all and is a property of the model, not of a host;
containment is whether a named hard gate then rejected it. A containment
rate quoted without the compliance rate it was conditioned on is not
interpretable, and zero compliance means containment was not exercised
rather than that it was perfect.
Pairs with docs/prompt-injection-resistance.md, which states the claim and
now names this as the measurement behind it.
A refusal is split again by what it was about. A document refused with a
diagnostic naming the injected reach is evidence about confinement; a
document refused for an unrelated syntax error kept the behaviour out and is
evidence about nothing. The two are counted apart, because folding them
together is how this column would come out flattering by accident.

columns.note: Output tokens spent per admitted component.
Per-candidate cost of gating a dynamically discovered tool.

hosts.name: raw Cordis / TypeScript
asymmetry: This host is scored on leaks rather than on compile-rate because TypeScript always
compiles. The asymmetry is not hidden and is not a flaw in the method: it is the
finding. There is no first-pass compile number to put in this row, because the number
would be 100% for every attempt including the ones that leak on unload.
The consequence for the table is that 'admits' and 'residue' are not two views of one
quantity. A reader comparing them across hosts is comparing different questions.

hosts.name: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk
selection_criteria: Has a plugin or tool registration lifecycle with an unload path. A framework with no
unload cannot fail the residue column honestly: it would score maximally badly by
construction, for a reason that says nothing about the runtime comparison.
Installable at a pinned version, so a reader gets the same code we ran.
Drivable by the same briefs in bench/specs.json without rewriting the task.
Third-party, so the comparison is not this repository against itself.
selected_because: Criterion 1, an unload path: McpServer.registerTool returns a handle whose
remove() deletes the registration and sends notifications/tools/list_changed,
and the host itself has close(). The claim is checked rather than asserted:
dist/esm/server/mcp.d.ts:289 in the published 1.30.0 artifact and fails if it
Criterion 3, drivable by the same briefs: the 30 briefs are 'provide these
operations, acquire a host resource, release it when you go away'. A tool
registration with a declared input schema is the same shape, and the same
The reason it is worth measuring rather than a foregone conclusion: remove()
is name-scoped, not resource-scoped. It deletes the registry entry and calls
nothing on the handler, so a tool that took something at registration has no
callback in which to give it back. That is a residue question with a real
answer, which is what this column needs.

rejected.name: langchain 1.5.11 and langchain-core 1.6.3
rejected.why: fails criterion 1. Tools are a constructor argument or a bind_tools result; the survey finds none of eight de-registration names on the published surface. Scoring its residue would score the absence of an API, which says nothing about a runtime comparison.

rejected.name: @openai/agents 0.18.0
rejected.why: fails criterion 1, same shape: tools are constructor state.

rejected.name: crewai 1.15.22
rejected.why: fails criterion 1 for tools. It does publish an event-bus unregister, which retires an event handler and not a tool.

rejected.name: semantic-kernel 1.44.1
rejected.why: the expected pick, and it fails criterion 1. It is the one mainstream framework that calls its unit a plugin, and it publishes add_plugin with no counterpart: the registry is a plain dict field, so a caller who wants removal mutates it, and no plugin is ever told it was removed.

rejected.name: pydantic-ai-slim 2.46.0
rejected.why: the runner-up, and it passes criterion 1 at a coarser grain: AbstractToolset.__aexit__ is a documented teardown, but it is scoped to the toolset rather than to a registration, and for_run_step hands lifecycle transitions back to the caller. A residue number under a scope-exit teardown answers a different question than one under a per-registration retirement, so both are not comparable in one column and the finer-grained host was taken.

honest_about_the_pick: This is a tool host rather than an agent framework in the LangChain sense, and
that is a real difference from the wording of the criterion. It is named here
because the criterion that discriminates is the unload path, and among the
popular hosts surveyed it is the only one with a per-registration one. The
alternative reading of the survey is also a finding and is stated in the
report: of six popular agent frameworks, none publishes a way to retire a
blocked_on: Running it needs an MCP host harness that registers a tool per brief, calls
remove(), and hands the result to a residue probe, plus a pinned-model
generation pass over the 30 briefs in MCP form. Neither exists, so every
framework cell is not-run rather than a number. Naming a host is not running
one and the report distinguishes the two.

hosts.kind: gated: G1-G9 plus the no-residue proof at compile time
